title: Mercury: The Closest Planet
summary: What makes Mercury, the smallest planet and the one closest to the Sun, a world of fast years, long days, extreme temperatures, and hidden ice.
poll: Mercury would be an exciting place for people to explore in person.

versions.title: Mercury
versions.text:
Look at the sky as the Sun sets. Look low. You may see a small dot. That dot is Mercury! It is hard to see. It stays near the Sun.

Mercury is a planet. It is the closest planet to the Sun. It is the smallest one, too. It is not much bigger than our Moon. It has no moons.

It zooms round the Sun. One trip takes 88 days. That is its year. But it spins very slow. A day there is longer than its year!

It has almost no air. Air is like a blanket. It keeps heat in. So heat gets out fast. So the days are hot. They are hot enough to melt lead. The nights are cold. They are far colder than ice.

Still, it is not the hottest planet. Venus is.

It is gray. It is full of rock. It has lots of craters. Craters are big holes. Rocks from space made them.

Ships from Earth have gone there. One found ice! It is in deep craters. The Sun does not shine there.

Mercury has almost no air. Air is like a blanket that holds in heat. With no blanket, the heat gets out. So the days get very hot. They are hot enough to melt lead. The nights are much colder than ice.

Still, it is not the hottest planet. Venus is even hotter.

Mercury is gray and full of rocks. It has lots of craters. These are big holes made when space rocks hit it.

Ships from Earth have flown to Mercury. One found ice! It hides in deep craters. The Sun never shines there.

versions.title: Mercury: The Closest Planet
versions.text:
Just after sunset, look low in the western sky. You may spot a small, bright point of light that does not twinkle. That light could be Mercury, the planet closest to the Sun.

Mercury is the smallest of the eight planets. It is only a little bigger than our Moon, and it has no moons of its own.

Mercury moves on a path, or orbit, around the Sun. It is faster than any other planet, so one orbit takes just 88 Earth days. That means a year on Mercury is very short. Yet Mercury spins very slowly. The time from one sunrise to the next is about 176 days, which is longer than its whole year!

Mercury has almost no atmosphere. On Earth, the atmosphere works like a blanket that holds in heat. Because Mercury has no blanket, its temperature swings wildly. In the day, the ground can reach about 430 degrees Celsius, which is hot enough to melt lead. At night, it can drop to about minus 180 degrees.

Still, Mercury is not the hottest planet. Venus is hotter, because its thick atmosphere traps heat.

Mercury is a gray, rocky world. Its ground is covered with craters made by crashing space rocks. When spacecraft visited, they found ice hidden in deep craters near its poles, in shadow that sunlight never reaches.

versions.title: Mercury: The Closest Planet
versions.text:
Just after sunset, look low in the western sky. You may spot a small, bright point of light that does not twinkle. That light could be Mercury, the planet that sits closest to the Sun.

Mercury is the smallest of the eight planets in our solar system. It is only slightly bigger than our Moon, and it has no moons of its own.

Like every planet, Mercury travels on a path, or orbit, around the Sun. It moves faster than any other planet, so a complete orbit takes just 88 Earth days. That means a year on Mercury is very short. Mercury spins extremely slowly, however. The time from one sunrise to the next is about 176 Earth days, which is longer than its entire year!

Mercury has almost no atmosphere. On Earth, the atmosphere works like a blanket that holds in heat. Because Mercury lacks this blanket, its temperature swings wildly between day and night. In daylight, the ground can reach about 430 degrees Celsius, which is hot enough to melt lead. After dark, it can plunge to about minus 180 degrees.

Surprisingly, Mercury is not the hottest planet. Venus is even hotter, because its thick atmosphere traps the heat.

Mercury is a gray, rocky world scarred by craters from crashing space rocks. When spacecraft visited, they discovered ice hidden inside deep craters near the poles, in permanent shadow where sunlight never reaches.

Reaching Mercury is harder than it sounds. A spacecraft heading toward the Sun keeps speeding up, so it must fly past other planets and use their pull to slow down.

versions.title: Mercury: A World of Extremes
versions.text:

Mercury is the smallest of the eight planets in our solar system. It is only slightly larger than our Moon, and unlike Earth, it has no moons of its own.

Like every planet, Mercury travels along a path, or orbit, around the Sun. Because it moves faster than any other planet, a complete orbit takes only 88 Earth days, so a year on Mercury is very short. Mercury rotates extremely slowly, however. The time from one sunrise to the next is about 176 Earth days, so a single day there lasts longer than an entire year!

Mercury has almost no atmosphere. On Earth, the atmosphere behaves like a blanket that holds in warmth. Because Mercury lacks this protective blanket, its temperature swings dramatically between day and night. In daylight, the ground can reach about 430 degrees Celsius, which is hot enough to melt lead, but after dark it can plunge to about minus 180 degrees.

Surprisingly, Mercury is not the hottest planet. Venus is even hotter, because its thick atmosphere traps heat.

Mercury is a gray, rocky world scarred by countless craters from crashing space rocks. When spacecraft explored it, scientists discovered ice hidden inside deep craters near the poles, where permanent shadow keeps sunlight away.

Reaching Mercury is surprisingly difficult. A spacecraft falling toward the Sun keeps gaining speed, so engineers send it past other planets, using their gravity to slow it down before it arrives.

Because Mercury lacks this protective blanket, its temperature swings dramatically between day and night. In daylight, the surface can reach approximately 430 degrees Celsius, which is hot enough to melt lead, but after dark it can plunge to roughly minus 180 degrees.

Surprisingly, Mercury is not the hottest planet. Venus is even hotter, because its dense atmosphere traps heat.

versions.title: Mercury: The Closest Planet
versions.text:
Just after sunset, look low toward the western horizon, and you may notice a small, bright point of light that does not twinkle. That light could be Mercury, the planet that orbits closest to the Sun and one that astronomers consider among the most difficult to observe, because it never strays far from the Sun's glare.

Mercury is the smallest of the eight planets in our solar system. It is only slightly larger than our Moon, and unlike Earth, it possesses no moons of its own.

Like every planet, Mercury travels along a path, or orbit, around the Sun. Because it moves faster than any other planet, a complete orbit requires only 88 Earth days, which makes a Mercurian year remarkably brief. Its rotation, however, is extremely slow, so the interval from one sunrise to the next is approximately 176 Earth days, and a single day there therefore lasts longer than an entire year.

Mercury has almost no atmosphere. On Earth, the atmosphere behaves like a blanket that retains warmth. Because Mercury lacks this protective layer, it experiences extreme temperature swings. In daylight, the surface can reach approximately 430 degrees Celsius, which is hot enough to melt lead, yet after dark it can plunge to roughly minus 180 degrees.

Surprisingly, Mercury is not the hottest planet. Venus is even hotter, because its dense atmosphere traps heat like a greenhouse.

Mercury is a gray, rocky world scarred by countless craters from colliding space rocks. When the MESSENGER mission orbited the planet between 2011 and 2015, scientists confirmed that ice is concealed inside deep craters near the poles, where permanent shadow prevents sunlight from ever reaching the frozen water.

Reaching Mercury is surprisingly difficult, because a spacecraft falling toward the Sun continually gains speed. Engineers therefore guide it past other planets several times, using their gravity as a natural brake before it finally arrives, which is why a newer mission called BepiColombo, launched in 2018, needed years to complete its journey.

versions.text:
Just after sunset, look low toward the western horizon, and you may notice a small, bright point of light that does not twinkle. That light could be Mercury, the planet that orbits closest to the Sun and one that astronomers consider among the most challenging to observe, because it never strays far from the Sun's overwhelming glare and consequently appears only briefly near dawn or dusk.

Its rotation, however, is extraordinarily sluggish, so the interval separating one sunrise from the next is approximately 176 Earth days, meaning that a single Mercurian day actually outlasts an entire Mercurian year.

In daylight, the surface can reach approximately 430 degrees Celsius, which is sufficiently hot to melt lead, yet after dark it can plummet to roughly minus 180 degrees, considerably colder than any location ever recorded on Earth.

When the MESSENGER mission orbited the planet between 2011 and 2015, scientists confirmed that ice is concealed inside deep craters near the poles, where permanent shadow prevents sunlight from ever reaching the frozen water.

Reaching Mercury is unexpectedly difficult, because a spacecraft descending toward the Sun continually accelerates. Engineers therefore navigate it past other planets several times, exploiting their gravity as a natural brake before it finally arrives, which explains why a more recent mission called BepiColombo, launched in 2018, required many years to complete its complicated journey to this mysterious and contradictory world.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: What Mercury is like and why it is special
How to build a spaceship and fly it to the Moon
Why Earth has only one moon and Mercury has none
How people go about their daily lives on Venus
questions.why: Every part of the article tells a fact about Mercury: its size, its year and day, its heat and cold, and its craters.

wrong.B: The article does not explain how to build a spaceship.
wrong.C: Earth's Moon is only used to compare size.
wrong.D: No people live on Venus, and Venus is only mentioned once.

88 days
176 years

wrong.A: One trip is much longer than one day.
wrong.B: Mercury is faster than Earth, so its year is shorter than ours.
wrong.D: The article does not say anything takes 176 years.

wrong.C: The article does not mention rivers.

wrong.C: The article says Mercury has no moons.

checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two facts from the article.

LOW.modelAnswer: I would not like to visit Mercury, because it has no blanket of atmosphere to hold in heat, so its temperature swings from very hot to very cold. It is also covered with craters from crashing space rocks, which would make it a dangerous, rocky planet to walk around. Mercury is the closest and smallest planet, but that does not make it a safe place to visit.

MID.prompt: Mercury is close to the Sun, yet it has ice. Explain how this is possible, using the words atmosphere and shadow.

MID.modelAnswer: Even though Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun, it still has ice because it has almost no atmosphere to spread heat around the planet. Deep inside some craters near its poles, there are patches of permanent shadow that sunlight never reaches, so those spots stay freezing cold. When spacecraft explored these dark craters, they found ice hidden safely in the shadow, away from Mercury's blazing daytime temperature.

HIGH.prompt: Mercury is called a world of extremes. Explain what this means, using at least three details from the article.
checklist: I explained what "world of extremes" means.
I used at least three details from the article.
I organized my explanation in clear, complete sentences.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Mercury is called a world of extremes because nearly everything about it swings between opposite ends with nothing in between. Its rotation is extremely slow, so one day lasts about 176 Earth days, which is longer than its entire 88-day orbit around the Sun. Without an atmosphere to trap or spread heat, its daytime temperature can reach 430 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead, while nighttime temperatures plunge to minus 180 degrees. Yet even on this scorching world, a spacecraft mission to study it found ice hidden in permanently shadowed craters near the poles, showing just how extreme and contradictory Mercury truly is.
